newsitem.title: UK: European economy resilient to dollar drama - so far.
newsitem.headline: European economy resilient to dollar drama - so far.

text.p: By Jacqueline Thorpe,
Europe's fragile economic recovery could be snuffed out by a retrenchment of the dollar but the currency's weakness so far was no cause for alarm, analysts said on Friday.
While the dollar has been hammered by the yen, its fall against the mark has been far less severe, allowing Europe to continue to claw its way out of an economic downturn on a wave of exports.

"I don't think the turn in the dollar we've seen against the European currencies so far is of particular concern," said Ian MaCafferty, director of international economics at NatWest Capital Markets in London.
"Small movements tend to be reflected more in changes in profit margins than they do in volumes," he said.
The dollar has certainly been suffering on world currency markets.
It has lost just under 10 percent of its value against the yen from a 55-month high of 127.46 on May 1. By 1049 GMT, it was quoted at 115.55/60 yen.
Against the mark, it dropped to a 1.67 low on May 12 from a recent high of 1.74 but has since rebounded back to 1.70 marks.
Robert Prior, European economist at HSBC James Capel in London, said that was only a blip compared to the dollar's relentless advance from March 1995 and its recent spurt higher from the end of 1996.
He said HSBC James Capel's Ecu trade-weighted exchange rate had dropped around 10 percent since its recent peak at the end of 1996.
And that has been driving European economic growth as weaker currencies make exports cheaper on world markets.
"As a rough rule of thumb, a fall of 10 percent in the Ecu trade-weighted exchange rate in one year will tend to add around 3/4 percent to European growth in the following year," he said.
Prior said despite the dollar's recent stumble, fundamental factors argue for continued strength against European currencies.

"We still expect U.S. rates to go up and we don't expect the first Japanese rate rise to come through until the very end of this year," he said. "Likewise for German rates, we don't expect anything to come through until well into next year," he said.
Nevertheless, a major pullback in the dollar would be a disaster for European economies, analysts said, and could throw a spanner into the works of European Economic and Monetary Union.
With unemployment still sky high, domestic demand only lukewarm and manufacturing only just shifting into high gear, the rebound in exports was crucial for growth.
"At the moment, there is a big divergence between hopes and reality in Europe," said Julian Jessop, chief European economist at Nikko Securities (Europe).
"People are hoping there will be a strong recovery based largely on exports picking up with a stronger dollar, but the reality is still pretty dim, particularly for unemployment," he said.

McCafferty said NatWest was still waiting for the recovery to broaden out into domestic industry, particularly in Germany and France. "Were the dollar to turn around dramatically and the European currencies to appreciate in a significant fashion, then there is a danger of a repeat of 1995 when the recovery...proved unsustainable," he said.
But both McCafferty and Jessop did not see this happening unless the dollar sank below 160 to 155 marks.
